newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Loyalists warn against secret IRA deals.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Loyalists warn against secret IRA deals.

text.p: A Protestant Loyalist leader accused Britain on Monday of working secret deals with the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and warned that it was in danger of wrecking peace efforts in Northern Ireland.

Gary McMichael, who heads the political arm of pro-British UDA guerrillas, was speaking after a newspaper report said the IRA was operating an unofficial ceasefire to try to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, into peace talks.
Britain and Sinn Fein have denied this.

"If the government think that thay can slot Sinn Fein into negotiations over the heads of the other participants on the basis of a deal cobbled together secretly between the government and Sinn Fein they could risk actually ending the process," McMichael said.
McMichael said he believed Sinn Fein was seeking concessions as a reward for a new IRA ceasefire.
"That's not on...What kind of message does that send the others if they believe they can use force to change the goalposts," he told BBC radio.

The IRA's last attack in its guerrilla war against British rule of Northern Ireland was on October 7, when it bombed Britain's army headquarters in Northern Ireland, killing a soldier and injuring 30 people.
The Catholic guerrillas abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February this year, with the first of a series of bombings on the British mainland.
John Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's Social, Democratic and Labour Party, has ackowledged that he was holding talks with Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams to try to get the IRA to restore the truce.
But Britain said it would not drop its preconditions for Sinn Fein's admission to the peace talks.
Baronness Jean Denton, a British minister for Northern Ireland, told BBC radio that Britain demanded a dependable IRA ceasefire and said this would not involve doing deals.
"Northern Ireland's future is going to be decided by the consent of the Northern Ireland people," she said.

The report in Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper came after a month of conflicting reports suggesting on the one hand that the IRA was planning a pre-Christmas bombing blitz and on the other that it was operating a new truce.
Recent comments by Sinn Fein and Britain have been seen as efforts to salvage the peace process chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell.
Britain has signalled it wants all-party negotiations on a political settlement and that disarmament could happen in tandem with the talks.

But pro-British Unionist parties are demanding that the IRA hand over weapons before Sinn Fein is allowed in. Sinn Fein sees the demand for "arms decommissioning" as tantamount to asking for an IRA surrender.
The Irish Times said on Monday that the main Unionist parties, who speak for the bulk of the Protestant community, have toughened their demands on disarmament.
Pro-British "Loyalist" parties have been allowed into the talks because their guerrilla allies are observing a two-year-old truce in their battle to safeguard British rule.
